cohort.definition: Entry-level engineering hires into Palantir's two official engineering tracks: Dev (platform product engineering) and Delta/FDSE (customer-embedded engineering). Experienced hires are a separate cohort and are not described by this record.
cohort.role_family: Software engineering (Software Engineer / 'Dev' and Forward Deployed Software Engineer / 'Delta')
cohort.time_window: roles and process as publicly described through 2026

compensation_notes.statement: Palantir publishes no pay range on the sources checked for this record. Third-party aggregators carry user-reported compensation for these roles; those figures are anecdotal and this record does not rely on them.

data_sources.label: Palantir blog: 'Dev versus Delta' — the company's own description of its two engineering tracks
Palantir blog: a day in the life of a Forward Deployed Software Engineer
Community-compiled Palantir interview guide on GitHub, built from public sources and candidate reports (labeled non-official)
Third-party interview-prep summary of the FDSE loop (candidate-reported, labeled anecdotal)

entry_routes.accessibility_note: The direct entry route for students who can show building breadth plus customer-facing judgment; the decomposition round is the filter to prepare for.
The platform route; weights systems and coding depth more than customer scenarios, per compiled guides.
For students who miss the first window: a year of real shipping elsewhere is the standard recovery move.
entry_routes.route: Lateral in after a strong engineering internship or startup stint

entry_routes.accessibility_note: Less code-deep than Delta; suits analyst-leaning profiles. A different job, not an easier version of the same one.
entry_routes.route: Deployment Strategist (Echo) as an adjacent door

hiring_bar_summary.statement: Palantir's own framing: Deltas are measured on technical outcomes for one customer — deploying and customizing the platform against critical, messy problems — while Devs are measured on a capability used by many customers. The entry bar is evidence you can own an ambiguous problem end to end, not a pedigree line.

hiring_cadence.statement: No single annual application deadline for entry-level engineering was found on the public sources checked for this record; postings appear and close on the company's careers site, so current postings — not this record — are the source of truth for any given cycle.

interview_styles.statement: Decomposition: an intentionally vague operational problem that the candidate must scope, constrain and turn into an engineering plan out loud, with constraints added as they go — the signature FDSE round in candidate reports.
Behavioral and motivation questions are woven through stages rather than isolated in one round, per compiled candidate reports.

known_biases_of_data: No population sample exists for this record: every distribution is a qualitative reported pattern from official role descriptions and community-compiled candidate reports, not a measured share.
Candidate reports over-represent people who reached late stages and chose to write up their experience; rejected-at-screen candidates are largely invisible (survivorship bias).
Palantir's own blog is a recruiting surface: it describes the roles as the company wants them understood, which may differ from day-to-day reality.

entries.label: Computer science, mathematics, engineering
entries.note: Compiled guides list these as the common majors among engineering hires; no measured mix is published.

entries.label: Economics, physics and other quantitative fields
entries.note: Compiled guides note a smaller presence from other quantitative fields; reported pattern only.

path_patterns.pattern: Dev route: join platform engineering and build one capability used by many customers
Delta route: join as an FDSE, embed with a single customer and deliver many capabilities for them
Adjacent route in via Deployment Strategist (Echo), the product-and-strategy-leaning embedded role, for candidates stronger on analysis than on code depth

entries.label: Military or government service (noted for FDSE)
entries.note: Role guides describe military and government backgrounds as a recurring feeder into forward-deployed work, consistent with Palantir's own account of FDSEs serving defense customers; no sourced share exists.

entries.label: Startups and engineering-heavy employers
entries.note: Candidate-reported pattern in compiled interview guides: lateral hires often arrive from startups or engineering-heavy teams; not measured.

process_stages.description: Everyone starts with one or two phone interviews covering background and motivation; candidate reports treat this as a real filter, not a formality.
A live coding screen (sometimes run through a third-party platform) or an online assessment mixing coding with data tasks, as commonly reported by candidates.
Several rounds drawn from a pool that candidate reports list as decomposition, coding, learning / re-engineering and system design; FDSE candidates most often report the decomposition round.
A final conversation with the hiring manager, reported to re-probe the weakest area from the onsite and to test project depth and values fit.

red_flags.statement: Government and defense customers are core to the business — Palantir's own FDSE account centers on a US Department of Defense customer. Candidates unwilling to do that work should self-select before investing in the process.
FDSE work means travel and time embedded at customer sites; it is not a remote platform job with a different title.

referral_weight_notes.statement: No official statement quantifying referral weight was found in the sources checked for this record. Treat any claim that a referral bypasses a screen as anecdotal; the documented screens above still apply.

entries.label: Top computer-science programs
entries.note: Community-compiled guides describe a visible concentration of hires from top CS programs, but no population share is published in any public source checked for this record — reported pattern only, not a measured distribution.

entries.label: Non-target schools with standout building evidence
entries.note: The same guides describe a visible minority entering from non-target schools on the strength of unusual projects or prior service — reported pattern only.

revealed.statement: Candidate reports compiled from public sources describe mission alignment being screened from the first recruiter conversation, and the decomposition round carrying the most weight for FDSE candidates — reported pattern, not firm policy.

Third-party prep summaries report that the coding rounds are practical rather than maximally algorithmic, and that candidates are tripped up by problem-scoping rounds more than by code difficulty — anecdotal, labeled as such.

stated.statement: Two distinct engineering tracks are screened differently: Dev (one capability, many customers) versus Delta (one customer, many capabilities).
FDSE work officially spans software development, data engineering, customer engagement and creative problem-solving, implemented together with end users.

entries.label: Decomposing ambiguous operational problems
entries.note: Candidate reports consistently name the decomposition round — scoping a messy real-world problem out loud — as the signature FDSE filter; labeled reported, from third-party prep summaries.

entries.label: Building real systems end to end
entries.note: Palantir's own FDSE account spans software development, data engineering and implementing solutions with end users — breadth across the stack rather than one specialty.

entries.label: Communicating with non-technical stakeholders
entries.note: The FDSE role as Palantir describes it requires engaging customers directly and translating between operators and engineers.

thesis_text: Palantir hires engineers into two officially distinct tracks: Devs build one capability for many customers, Deltas embed with one customer and deliver many capabilities for them. For a new graduate the honest read is that the screen is about owning ambiguous problems end to end — decomposing a messy operational situation, building across the stack, and communicating with the people who will use the thing. No population data on who gets in is published in the public sources checked, so this record states patterns qualitatively and labels candidate-reported process details as reported, never as firm policy.

values_culture_signals.statement: Palantir frames Delta success as impact on the customer's goal — ownership of an outcome in someone else's operation, often in defense, healthcare or industry settings.
Compiled candidate reports describe explicit screening for genuine interest in the company's mission and comfort with the ethics of government and defense work — reported, not published policy.
